¶
'''2.''' Conceding or allowing that; however true it be that; even were it the case that; even if: followed by a subjunctive clause noting a mere possibility or supposition.

{{smaller block|I parfourned the penaunce the preest me enioyned,
And am ful sori for my synnes, and so I shal euere
Whan I thinke there-on, ''theighe'' I were a pope.
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), v. 609.}}}}

{{smaller block|We . . . charge noght his chateryng, ''thogh'' he chide euer.
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1931.}}}}

{{smaller block|Nay, take all,
''Though'' 'twere my exhibition to a royal
For one whole year.
{{right|''Fletcher'', Spanish Curate, i. 1.}}}}

{{smaller block|What would it avail us to have a hireling Clergy, ''though'' never so learned?
{{right|''Milton'', On Def. of Humb. Remonst.}}}}

'''3.''' Hence, without concessive force, in the case that; if: commonly used in the expression ''as though''.

{{smaller block|And schalle be youre Deffence in all aduerssite,
''As though'' that y were dayly in youre sight.
{{right|''Political Poems'', etc. (ed. Furnivall), p. 40.}}}}

{{smaller block|In the vine were three branches, and it was ''as though'' it budded.
{{right|Gen. xl. 10.}}}}

{{smaller block|O, how can Love's eye be true,
That is so vex'd with watching and with tears?
No marvel, then, ''though'' I mistake my view.
{{right|''Shak.'', Sonnets, cxlviii.}}}}

{{smaller block|The beauty of her flesh abash'd the boy,
''As tho''' it were the beauty of her soul.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Pelleas and Ettarre.}}}}

'''4.''' Nevertheless; however; still; but: followed by a clause restricting or modifying preceding statements.

{{smaller block|I will be here again, even ''with a thought.''
{{right|''Shak.'', J. C., v. 3. 19.}}}}

'''What is my thought like?''' a game in which one or more of the players think of a certain object, and the rest, through questions as to what that thought or object is like, try to guess it. ={{sc|Syn.}} '''1.''' (''a'') ''Feeling'', etc. (see ''sentiment''); imagination, supposition.

'''thought<sup>2</sup>''' (thât). Preterit and past participle of ''think''<sup>1</sup>.

'''thought<sup>3</sup>''' (thât). Preterit of ''think''<sup>2</sup>.

'''thought<sup>4</sup>''' (thât), ''n.'' [Also ''thowt;'' dial. form of ''thoft''<sup>1</sup>; in part a corruption of ''thwart''<sup>1</sup>.] A rower's seat; a thwart. [Prov. Eng.]

{{smaller block|The ''thoughts'', the seats of rowers in a boat.
{{right|''Dict. ap. Moor.'' (''Halliwell'', under ''thowts.'')}}}}

'''thoughted''' (thâ′ted), ''a.'' [< ''thought''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.] Having thoughts: used chiefly in composition with a qualifying word.

{{smaller block|Low-''thoughted'' care.
{{right|''Milton'', Comus, l. 6.}}}}

{{smaller block|Those whom passion hath not blinded,
Subtle-''thoughted'', myriad-minded.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Ode to Memory.}}}}

{{smaller block|Shallow-''thoughted'', and cold-hearted.
{{right|''H. Spencer'', Universal Progress, p. 102.}}}}

'''thoughten†''' (thâ′tn). An old preterit plural (and irregular past participle) of ''think''<sup>1</sup>.

{{smaller block|Be you ''thoughten''
That I came with no ill intent.
{{right|''Shak.'', Pericles, iv. 6. 115.}}}}

'''thought-executing''' (thât′ek″sē-kū-ting), ''a.'' Effective with the swiftness of thought. Compare ''upon a thought'', under ''thought''<sup>1</sup>.

{{smaller block|You sulphurous and ''thought-executing'' fires,
Vaunt-couriers to oak-cleaving thunderbolts!
{{right|''Shak.'', Lear, iii. 2. 4.}}}}

¶
'''thoughtful''' (thât′fu̇l), ''a.'' [< ME. ''thoughtful, thohtful, thoȝtful''; < ''thought''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ful''.] 1. Occupied with thought; engaged in or disposed to reflection; contemplative; meditative.

{{smaller block|On these he mus'd within his ''thoughtful'' mind.
{{right|''Dryden'', Æneid, vii. 347.}}}}

{{smaller block|No circumstance is more characteristic of an educated and ''thoughtful'' man than that he is ready, from time to time, to review his moral judgements.
{{right|''Fowler'', Shaftesbury and Hutcheson, p. 91.}}}}

2. Characterized by or manifesting thought; pertaining to thought; concerned with or dedicated to thought.

{{smaller block|War, horrid war, your ''thoughtful'' walks invades,
And steel now glitters in the Muses' shades.
{{right|''Pope'', Choruses to Tragedy of Brutus, i. 7.}}}}

{{smaller block|Much in vain, my zealous mind
Would to learned Wisdom's throne
Dedicate each ''thoughtful'' hour.
{{right|''Akenside'', Odes, ii. 9.}}}}

{{smaller block|His coloring (in so far as one can judge of it by reproduction) is pleasing if not perceptibly ''thoughtful.''
{{right|''The Nation'', XLVII. 460.}}}}

3. Mindful, as to something specified; heedful; careful: followed by ''of'' or an infinitive.

{{smaller block|For this they have been ''thoughtful'' to invest
Their sons with arts and martial exercises.
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., iv. 5. 73.}}}}

{{smaller block|''Thoughtful of'' thy gain,
Not ''of'' my own.
{{right|''J. Philips'', Cider, i. 364.}}}}

4. Showing regard or consideration for others; benevolent; considerate; kindly.

{{right|''Stubbes'', Christal Glasse (New Shak. Soc.), p. 198.}}
Taunt him with the license of ink: if thou ''thou'st'' him some thrice, it shall not be amiss. ''Shak.'', T. N., iii. 2. 48.}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To use ''thou'', ''thee'', ''thy'', and ''thine'' in discourse, as do the Friends.

'''though''' (ᴛ̵ʜō), ''conj.'' and ''adv.'' [Also written briefly ''tho''', ''tho''; < ME. ''though'', ''thoughe'', ''thogh'', ''thoȝ'', ''thoh'', ''thow'', ''thoo'', ''tho'', ''thauh'', ''thaȝ'', ''thau'', ''thaih'', ''theȝ'', ''thei'', ''theiȝ'', ''theiȝh'', etc., < AS. ''theáh'', ''thēh'' = OS. ''thōh'' = OFries. ''thāch'' = D. ''doch'' = MLG. ''doch'' = OHG. ''dōh'', ''doh'', MHG. ''doch'', G. ''doch'' = Icel. ''thō'' = Sw. ''dock'' = Dan. ''dog'' = Goth. ''thauh'', though (the Goth. form indicating a formation < *''tha'', pronominal base of ''that'', etc., + ''-uh'', an enclitic particle).] '''I.''' ''conj.'' '''1.''' Notwithstanding that; in spite of the fact that; albeit; while: followed by a clause, usually indicative, either completely or elliptically expressed, and noting a recognized fact.

{{smaller block|''Thog'' the asse spac, frigtede he [Balaam] nogt.
{{right|''Genesis and Exodus'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 3978.}}
''Thaȝ'' Arther the hende kyng at herte hade wonder,
He let no semblaunt be sene.
{{right|''Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 467.}}
This child, ''the'' hit were ȝung, wel hit understod,
For seli child is sone i-lered ther he wole beo god.
{{right|''Life of Thomas Beket'', p. 8. (''Halliwell.'')}}
He's young and handsome, ''though'' he be my brother.
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Scornful Lady, iii. 2.}}
Her plans, ''though'' vast, were never visionary.
{{right|''Prescott'', Ferd. and Isa., ii. 16.}}}}

'''2.''' Conceding or allowing that; however true it be that; even were it the case that; even if: followed by a subjunctive clause noting a mere possibility or supposition.

{{smaller block|I parfourned the penaunce the preest me enioyned,
And am ful sori for my synnes, and so I shal euere
Whan I thinke there-on, ''theighe'' I were a pope.

{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1931.}}}}

{{smaller block|Nay, take all,

{{right|''Milton'', On Def. of Humb. Remonst.}}}}

'''3.''' Hence, without concessive force, in the case that; if: commonly used in the expression ''as though''.

{{smaller block|And schalle be youre Deffence in all aduerssite,
''As though'' that y were dayly in youre sight.
{{right|''Political Poems'', etc. (ed. Furnivall), p. 40.}}}}

{{smaller block|In the vine were three branches, and it was ''as though'' it budded.

{{smaller block|The beauty of her flesh abash'd the boy,
''As tho''' it were the beauty of her soul.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Pelleas and Ettarre.}}}}

'''4.''' Nevertheless; however; still; but: followed by a clause restricting or modifying preceding statements.

{{smaller block|Lecherie . . . is on of the zeuen dyadliche zennes, ''thaȝ'' ther by zome bronches thet ne byeth naȝt dyadlich zenne.
{{right|''Ayenbite of Inwyt'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 9.}}}}

{{smaller block|Glad shall I be if I meet with no more such brunts; ''though'' I fear we are not got beyond all danger.
{{right|''Bunyan'', Pilgrim's Progress, i.}}}}

'''As though.''' See def. 3.—'''Though that†''', though.

{{smaller block|''Though that'' my death were adjunct to my act,
By heaven, I would do it. {{right|''Shak.'', K. John, iii. 3. 57.}}}}

'''What though''' (elliptically for ''what though the fact'' or ''case is so''), what does that matter? what does it signify? need I (we, you, etc.) care about that?

{{smaller block|I keep but three men, . . . but ''what though?'' yet I live like a poor gentleman born. {{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., i. 1. 286.}}}}

{{smaller|='''Syn.''' ''Although, Though'', etc. (See ''although''.) ''While, Though.'' See ''while''.}}

'''II.''' ''adv.'' Notwithstanding this or that; however; for all that.

{{smaller block|Would Katharine had never seen him ''though!''
{{right|''Shak.'', T. of the S., iii. 2. 26.}}}}

{{smaller block|I' faith, Sneer, ''though'', I am afraid we were a little too severe on Sir Fretful. {{right|''Sheridan'', The Critic, i. 1.}}}}

'''though-all†''' (ᴛ̵ʜō′âl), ''conj.'' [ME. ''though al, thof al'', etc.; < ''though'' + ''all''. Cf. ''although''.] Although.

{{smaller block|I am but a symple knave,
''Thof all'' I come of curtayse kynne.
{{right|''York Plays'', p. 121.}}}}

{{smaller block|Nowe loke on me, my lorde dere,
''Thof all'' I put me noght in pres.
{{right|''York Plays'', p. 122.}}}}

'''thoughless†''' (ᴛ̵ʜō′les), ''conj.'' [ME. ''thaȝles''; < ''though'' + ''-less'' as in ''unless''.] Nevertheless; still; however. {{smaller block|''Thaȝles'' the wone is kueaduol, and may wel wende to zenne dyadlich. {{right|''Ayenbite of Inwyt'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 6.}}}}

'''thought'''<sup>1</sup> (thât), ''n.'' [< ME. ''thought, thouht, thoht, thoȝt, thuȝt, ithoȝt,'' < AS. ''gethōht,'' also ''theaht, getheaht'' = OS. ''githāht,'' f., thinking, belief, = D. ''gedachte'' = OHG. *''daht,'' MHG. ''dāht,'' f., thought, OHG. ''gedāht'' (cf. OHG. ''anadāht,'' MHG. ''andāht,'' G. ''andacht,'' attention, devotion (= Goth. ''andathahts,'' attention), G. ''bedacht,'' deliberation) = Icel. ''thōtti, thōttr,'' thought, = Goth. ''thuhtus,'' thought (the above forms being more or less confused); with formative ''-t'' or ''-tu,'' < AS. ''thencan'' (pret. ''thōhte''), etc., think: see ''think''<sup>1</sup>.] 1. The act or the product of thinking. {{smaller|Psychologically considered, thought has two elements—one a series of phenomena of consciousness during an interval of time in which there is no noticeable interruption of the current of association by outward reactions (peripheral sensations and muscular efforts); the other a more or less definite acquisition to the stock of mental possessions—namely, a notion, which may repeatedly present itself and be recognized as identical. The former of these elements is the act of thinking as it appears to consciousness; the latter is the lasting effect produced upon the mind, likewise considered from the point of view of consciousness. (''a'') In the most concrete sense, a single step in a process of thinking; a notion; a reflection.}}

{{smaller block|"They are never alone," said I, "that are accompanied with noble ''thoughts.''" {{right|''Sir P. Sidney,'' Arcadia, i.}}}}

{{smaller block|Truth shall nurse her,
Holy and heavenly ''thoughts'' still counsel her.
{{right|''Shak.,'' Hen. VIII., v. 5. 30.}}}}

{{smaller block|Some to Conceit alone their taste confine,
And glittering ''thoughts'' struck out at every line.
{{right|''Pope,'' Essay on Criticism, l. 290.}}}}

{{smaller block|To me the meanest flower that blows can give
''Thoughts'' that do often lie too deep for tears.
{{right|''Wordsworth,'' Ode, Immortality.}}}}

(''b'') The condition or state of a person during such mental action.

{{smaller block|Horn sat upon the grunde,
In ''thuȝte'' he was ibunde.
{{right|''King Horn'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 32.}}
Sir Bedivere . . . paced beside the mere,
Counting the dewy pebbles, fix'd in ''thought.''
{{right|''Tennyson'', Morte d'Arthur.}}}}

(''c'') A synonym of ''cognition'' in the common threefold division of modes of consciousness: from the fact that ''thought'', as above described, embraces every cognitive process except sensation, which is a mode of consciousness more allied to volition than to other kinds of cognition.

{{smaller block|Feeling, ''thought'', and action are to a certain extent opposed or mutually exclusive states of mind.
{{right|''J. Sully'', Outlines of Psychol., p. 657.}}}}

(''d'') The objective element of the intellectual product.

{{smaller block|''Thought'' always proceeds from the less to the more determinate, and, in doing so, it cannot determine any object positively without determining it negatively, or determine it negatively without determining it positively.
{{right|''E. Caird'', Philos. of Kant, p. 313.}}
''Thought'' is, in every case, the cognition of an object, which really, actually, existentially out of ''thought'', is ideally, intellectually, intelligibly within it; and just because within in the latter sense, is it known as actually without in the former.
{{right|''Mind'', No. 35, July, 1884.}}}}

(''e'') A judgment or mental proposition, in which form the concept always appears.

{{smaller block|''Thought'' proper, as distinguished from other facts of consciousness, may be adequately described as the act of knowing or judging things by means of concepts.
{{right|''Dean Mansel'', Prolegomena to Logic, p. 22.}}}}

(''f'') An argument, inference, or process of reasoning, by which process the concept is always produced.

{{smaller block|Without entering upon the speculations of the Nominalists and the Realists, we must admit that, in the process of ratiocination, properly called ''thought'', the mind acts only by words.
{{right|''G. P. Marsh'', Lects. on Eng. Lang., i.}}}} (''g'') A concept, considered as something which, under the influence of experience and mental action, has a development of its own, more or less independent of individual caprices, and that (1) in the life of an individual, and (2) in history: as, the gradual development of Greek ''thought.'' (''h'') The subjective element of intellectual activity; thinking.

{{smaller block|By the word ''thought'' I understand all that which so takes place in us that we of ourselves are immediately conscious of it.
{{right|''Descartes'', Prin. of Philos. (tr. by Veitch), i. § 9.}}}}

{{smaller|(''i'') The understanding; intellect.}}

{{smaller block|For our instruction, to impart
Things above earthly ''thought''.
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., vii. 82.}}}}

{{smaller block|What never was seen or heard of may yet be conceived; nor is anything beyond the power of ''thought'' except what implies an absolute contradiction.
{{right|''Hume'', Inquiry concerning Human Understanding, ii.}}}}

2. An intention; a design; a purpose; also, a half-formed determination or expectation with reference to future action: with ''of'': as, I have some ''thought of'' going to Europe.

{{smaller block|They have not only ''thoughts of'' repentance, but general purposes of doing the acts of it at one time or other.
{{right|''Stillingfleet'', Sermons, II. iii.}}}}

{{smaller block|The sun was very low when we came to this place, and we had some ''thoughts of'' staying there all night; but the people gave us no great encouragement.
{{right|''Pococke'', Description of the East, II. i. 106.}}}}

3. ''pl.'' A particular frame of mind; a mood or temper.

{{smaller block|I would not there reside,
To put my father in impatient ''thoughts''
By being in his eye.
{{right|''Shak.'', Othello, i. 3. 243.}}}} It glads me

To find your ''thoughts'' so even.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Catiline, iii. 1.}}}}

4†. Doubt; perplexity.

{{smaller block|Whan the lordes vndirstod that kynge Arthur was gon and lefte his londe, than thei hadde grete ''thought'' wherefore it myght be; but no wise cowde thei devise the cause.
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), ii. 176.}}}}

5. Care; trouble; anxiety; grief.

{{smaller block|There is another thynge . . .
Which cause is of my deth for sorwe and ''thought.''
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, I. 579.}}

In this ''thought'' and this anguyssh was the mayden by the coniurison of Merlin. {{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), iii. 608.}}

Take no ''thought'' [be not anxious, R. V.] for your life, what ye shall eat, or what ye shall drink. {{right|Mat. vi. 25.}}

Gonzales was done to death by Gasca. Soto died of ''thought'' in Florida; and ciuill wars eate vp the rest in Peru. {{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 871.}}}}

6. A slight degree; a fraction; a trifle; a little: used in the adverbial phrase ''a thought:'' as, ''a thought'' too small.

{{smaller block|Here be they are every way as fair as she, and ''a thought'' fairer, I trow. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Cynthia's Revels, iv. 1.}}

Though I now totter, yet I think I am ''a thought'' better.
{{right|''Swift'', Letter, Aug. 12, 1727.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Elemental law of thought.''' See ''elemental.''—'''Free thought.''' See ''free.''—'''Objective thought.''' See ''objective reason'', under ''objective.''—'''Second thoughts''', maturer or calmer reflection; after-consideration: as, on ''second thoughts'', I will not speak of it.}}

{{smaller block|Is it so true that ''second thoughts'' are best?
Not first, and third, which are a riper first?
{{right|''Tennyson'', Sea Dreams.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Upon''' or '''with a thought''', with the speed of thought; in a twinkling; immediately.}}

{{smaller block|The fit is momentary; ''upon a thought''
He will again be well. {{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, iii. 4. 55.}} I will be here again, even ''with a thought.''
{{right|''Shak.'', J. C., v. 3. 19.}}}}

{{smaller block|The ''thoughts'', the seats of rowers in a boat.
{{right|''Dict. ap. Moor.'' (''Halliwell'', under ''thowts.'')}}}}

'''thoughted''' (thâ′ted), ''a.'' [< ''thought''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.] Having thoughts: used chiefly in composition with a qualifying word.

{{smaller block|Low-''thoughted'' care.
{{right|''Milton'', Comus, l. 6.}}}}

{{smaller block|Those whom passion hath not blinded,
Subtle-''thoughted'', myriad-minded.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Ode to Memory.}}}}

{{smaller block|Shallow-''thoughted'', and cold-hearted.
{{right|''H. Spencer'', Universal Progress, p. 102.}}}}

{{smaller block|Be you ''thoughten''

{{right|''Shak.'', Pericles, iv. 6. 115.}}}}

'''thoughtful''' (thât′fu̇l), ''a.'' [< ME. ''thoughtful, thohtful, thoȝtful''; < ''thought''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ful''.] 1. Occupied with thought; engaged in or disposed to reflection; contemplative; meditative.

{{smaller block|On these he mus'd within his ''thoughtful'' mind.
{{right|''Dryden'', Æneid, vii. 347.}}}}

{{smaller block|No circumstance is more characteristic of an educated and ''thoughtful'' man than that he is ready, from time to time, to review his moral judgements.
{{right|''Fowler'', Shaftesbury and Hutcheson, p. 91.}}}}

2. Characterized by or manifesting thought; pertaining to thought; concerned with or dedicated to thought.

{{smaller block|War, horrid war, your ''thoughtful'' walks invades,
And steel now glitters in the Muses' shades.
{{right|''Pope'', Choruses to Tragedy of Brutus, i. 7.}}}}

{{smaller block|Much in vain, my zealous mind
Would to learned Wisdom's throne
Dedicate each ''thoughtful'' hour.
{{right|''Akenside'', Odes, ii. 9.}}}}

{{smaller block|His coloring (in so far as one can judge of it by reproduction) is pleasing if not perceptibly ''thoughtful.''
{{right|''The Nation'', XLVII. 460.}}}}

3. Mindful, as to something specified; heedful; careful: followed by ''of'' or an infinitive.

{{smaller block|For this they have been ''thoughtful'' to invest
Their sons with arts and martial exercises.
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., iv. 5. 73.}}}}

{{smaller block|''Thoughtful of'' thy gain,
Not ''of'' my own.
{{right|''J. Philips'', Cider, i. 364.}}}}

4. Showing regard or consideration for others; benevolent; considerate; kindly.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
